title: Design System at Scale
prompt: Our company has 25 web apps built by 40 teams, and each has its own buttons, modals and colours. Design the design system and component library they should all share, and tell me how you would get them to adopt it.

clarify.q: Which frameworks do the 25 apps use? All React, or React plus Angular, Vue and server-rendered pages?
clarify.why: One framework lets us ship React components directly. Several frameworks push behaviour into tokens and CSS that everyone can use, and possibly web components, which costs more.

clarify.q: How many brands or themes: one brand with dark mode, or white-label products for several clients?
clarify.why: Many brands make the token architecture the core of the design. One brand means tokens are mostly a consistency tool.

clarify.q: Who staffs it, and is it mandated or opt-in?
clarify.why: A 6-person team with no mandate must win teams over with migration help and speed. A mandate changes the adoption plan, not the need for good tooling.

clarify.q: Is there a design source of truth today, such as a Figma library?
clarify.why: If design and code use different values, we need a token pipeline that keeps them in sync, or the system drifts again within a year.

clarify.q: What accessibility level must we meet, and is there legal pressure?
clarify.why: A WCAG 2.2 AA requirement, for example from a public-sector client or EU rules, makes accessibility a guarantee we test in CI, not a nice-to-have.

clarify.q: How do apps ship: one monorepo, many repos, micro-frontends on one page?
clarify.why: Micro-frontends on one page may load two versions of the library at once, so CSS and tokens must not clash between versions.

clarify.q: What does success look like in a year?
clarify.why: It defines the metrics: share of UI from the system, version lag, time to build a new screen, accessibility bug count.

functional: Design tokens (colour, spacing, type, radius, motion) from one source, published for web (CSS variables, TypeScript) and for Figma.
Light, dark and high-contrast themes, and brand themes, switchable at runtime without reloading.
A component library (about 60 components) with documented props, states and usage guidance.
Every breaking change ships with a deprecation period, a migration guide and an automated codemod.
A docs site with live examples, accessibility notes and a 'do / don't' for each component.
Dashboards that show adoption and version lag per app and per team.
nonFunctional: Accessibility: every stable component meets WCAG 2.2 AA for its documented usage, checked in CI on every pull request.
Tree-shakeable: an app pays only for the components it imports; a typical page adds under 30 KB gzipped of library JavaScript.
Theming adds no runtime JavaScript: switching theme is a CSS attribute change, under 1 frame of work.
Releases weekly; every release passes unit, interaction, axe and visual-regression tests.
Supports the current and previous major version for at least 6 months.
Works with server-side rendering and React Server Components (no window access at import time).
outOfScope: Rewriting every app's screens: we provide components and migration tools; teams own their screens.
Native iOS and Android component libraries (tokens are exported for them, components are not).
Page-level templates and content guidelines beyond component usage.

assumptions: 25 apps, 40 teams, ~300 frontend engineers; design system team of 6 engineers and 2 designers
60 components averaging 2 KB gzipped each; a typical page uses 12 of them
400 tokens in total; a theme overrides ~150 semantic tokens of ~45 bytes each
6 themes: light, dark, high contrast for 2 brands
Visual tests: ~8 stories per component, 3 themes, 2 viewports; ~0.5 s per screenshot

steps.label: Library JavaScript per page
steps.math: Tree-shaken: 12 × 2 KB = 24 KB. Not tree-shaken: 60 × 2 KB = 120 KB, so +96 KB ÷ 200 KB/s
steps.result: 24 KB vs 120 KB: broken tree-shaking costs ~0.5 s download on slow 4G, plus parse time

steps.label: Theme CSS cost
steps.math: 150 tokens × 45 B ≈ 6.8 KB raw ≈ 1.5 KB gzip per theme; 6 themes ≈ 9 KB gzip
steps.result: Tokens are cheap: ship all themes in one file and switch by attribute

steps.label: Support load
steps.math: 300 engineers × 1 question per month = 300 ÷ 20 working days
steps.result: ≈ 15 questions a day: docs, examples and lint rules must answer most of them, or 6 people drown

steps.label: Cost of one breaking change
steps.math: Manual: 2 days per app × 25 = 50 engineer-days. With a codemod covering 90%: 0.2 days review + 10% of 2 days manual = 0.4 days × 25
steps.result: ≈ 10 engineer-days instead of 50: every breaking change needs a codemod

steps.label: Visual regression per pull request
steps.math: 60 × 8 × 3 × 2 = 2 880 screenshots × 0.5 s = 1 440 s = 24 min; sharded over 8 workers
steps.result: ≈ 3 min: affordable on every pull request, but only if sharded and limited to changed components when possible

steps.label: Adoption scan
steps.math: 25 repos, nightly AST scan ~2 min each = 50 min of CI per night
steps.result: Cheap enough to run every night and trend per team

estimates.takeaway: The numbers say the real costs are people and migrations, not bytes. Tokens cost ~1.5 KB per theme, so theming should be pure CSS. Two things scale badly: support questions (~15 a day) and breaking changes (50 engineer-days each without codemods). So invest in docs, lint rules and codemods early. The one byte risk is broken tree-shaking, which costs ~96 KB per page.

api.returns: CSS custom properties on :root, overridden under [data-theme='dark'] and [data-brand='b']
api.note: Apps use semantic tokens only. Primitive tokens like --ds-blue-600 are private and may change in any minor version.

api.body: { variant: 'primary' | 'secondary' | 'danger' | 'ghost', size: 'sm' | 'md', loading?, disabled?, iconStart?, asChild? } + native button attributes
api.returns: A real <button> with focus ring, loading state announced via aria-busy
api.note: Closed variant set, no style props. asChild lets a team render a router link with button styling without wrapping.

api.returns: Modal with focus trap, focus return, Escape to close, inert background, scroll lock
api.note: title is required by the type, so an unlabelled dialog does not compile. open/onOpenChange or defaultOpen: controlled or uncontrolled.

api.body: import { Button } from '@acme/ui' or '@acme/ui/button'; import '@acme/ui/styles.css'; import tokens from '@acme/tokens'
api.returns: ESM only, one module per component, sideEffects limited to CSS files, typed
api.note: Subpath exports keep tree-shaking reliable even in bundlers that handle barrels badly.

api.returns: Rewritten files plus a report of spots it could not migrate, marked with TODO(ds-v7) comments
api.note: Each transform is tested against fixtures taken from real app code.

api.body: Internal dashboard API fed by the nightly scanner
api.returns: 200 { apps: [{ app, dsVersion, majorsBehind, dsElements, localEquivalents, coverage, a11yViolations }] }
api.note: Same data drives the leadership dashboard and the per-team weekly email.

entities.name: Token
entities.store: tokens/*.json in the monorepo (W3C design tokens format), synced with Figma variables
entities.why: One source builds CSS variables, TypeScript constants, Figma variables and native exports, so code and design can't drift.

entities.name: ComponentManifest
entities.store: Generated from source at build time
fields: keyboard model, roles, what the app must supply
entities.why: Docs, lint rules and the adoption scanner read the same facts about each component.

entities.name: AdoptionSnapshot
entities.store: Warehouse table, one row per app per night
fields: from axe runs in that app's CI
entities.why: Trends per team show where to help, and prove the system's value to leadership.

data.note: The client 'state' of a design system is small: the theme lives on <html data-theme data-brand>, chosen server-side from a cookie (so there is no flash of the wrong theme) and falling back to prefers-color-scheme. Components are stateless about theme. They only read CSS variables, which is why themes need no React context and work in server components. Each major version namespaces its CSS classes (ds7-button) so two versions on one micro-frontend page don't collide.

hld.summary:
Everything lives in one monorepo (pnpm workspaces with Turborepo or Nx): tokens, icons, ui (React components), codemods, eslint-plugin and the docs site. Designers edit variables in Figma; a sync job opens a pull request to the token JSON, so code review is the gate for design changes too. The token build emits CSS variables per theme, TypeScript constants and native formats.

Components are built in layers: behaviour hooks (focus, keyboard, ARIA), styled components on top using only semantic tokens, and a few compound components for complex widgets. CI runs unit, interaction, axe and visual tests per component. Changesets turn merged pull requests into weekly semver releases on the private npm registry. Apps consume packages; a bot opens upgrade pull requests with codemods applied. A nightly scanner reads every app repo and feeds the adoption dashboard.

diagram.title: Token pipeline, release and adoption loop
diagram.src:

flows.title: A designer changes the brand's primary colour
steps: Designer updates the semantic token in Figma variables.
Sync job opens a pull request changing color.action.primary in brand-b.json.
CI builds tokens, checks contrast ratios of all text/background token pairs (fails under 4.5:1), and runs visual tests that show every affected component.
Design and engineering approve; it ships in the weekly minor release.
Apps get it on their next upgrade with no code change, because they only use semantic tokens.

flows.title: Shipping a breaking change
steps: Release N (minor): old prop still works, logs a dev-only deprecation warning with a link, and the lint rule flags it.
Codemod is written and tested against fixtures copied from real app code.
Release N+1 (major, at most twice a year): old prop removed; changelog links the codemod.
Upgrade bot opens a pull request in each app with the codemod applied and a list of manual TODOs.
Dashboard tracks majors-behind per app; the previous major gets fixes for 6 months.

flows.title: Measuring adoption every night
steps: Scanner clones each app repo and parses source files with an AST parser.
Counts imports and JSX usage of @acme/ui components, deprecated props, and local look-alikes (raw button elements with classes, local Modal components).
Writes an AdoptionSnapshot row per app; pulls axe violation counts from each app's CI.
Dashboard shows coverage, version lag and trend per team; the weekly email highlights the biggest gaps.

deepDives.title: Design tokens and theming
deepDives.problem: Teams hard-code #1a73e8 in 3 000 places. Dark mode, a second brand, or a contrast fix then means touching every app. We need one place to change a colour, theme switching without a reload or a flash, and no runtime cost.

options.name: Sass or Less variables
options.how: Tokens compiled into each app's CSS at build time.
pros: Zero runtime; familiar
cons: A theme switch needs a second stylesheet and a reload
Each app must rebuild to get a token change

options.name: CSS-in-JS theme object
options.how: A ThemeProvider passes a JavaScript theme; styles are computed at runtime.
pros: Typed theme; dynamic values easy
cons: Runtime style work on every render
Awkward with server components and streaming

options.name: Tiered tokens built to CSS custom properties
options.how: Primitive tokens (gray-900), semantic tokens (text-default → gray-900, or gray-50 in dark), component tokens (button-bg → action-primary). Built to variables on :root, overridden under [data-theme] and [data-brand].
pros: Theme switch is one attribute change; zero JavaScript
Works in any framework, plain HTML and server components
One token change reaches every app
cons: Variables are untyped in CSS; a typo fails silently
Need tooling to stop teams using primitives directly

deepDives.choice: Tiered tokens built to CSS custom properties, from JSON in the W3C design tokens format. Apps may use semantic tokens only; a stylelint rule bans raw hex values and primitive tokens outside the library. A CI check computes contrast for every documented text/background pair in every theme. Theme is set server-side from a cookie on <html>, so there's no flash. Component tokens exist only where a component genuinely differs, otherwise the token count explodes. If the company had one brand and no dark mode, I'd still use CSS variables, just with a much smaller semantic layer.

deepDives.title: Component API philosophy
deepDives.problem: Every team wants their special case. Say yes to everything and the Button gets 40 props and 200 combinations nobody can test. Say no to everything and teams fork the component or write their own, and adoption dies.

options.name: Configuration-heavy components
options.how: One component per widget with many props: color, padding, iconPosition, shadow…
pros: Easy to discover in autocomplete
cons: Combinations explode; impossible to test or keep consistent
Style props let teams bypass the design language

options.name: Composition (compound components and slots)
options.how: Dialog.Content, Dialog.Title, Select.Option… Teams compose parts; each part has few props.
pros: Flexible without new props
Each part is small and testable
cons: More to learn
Teams can compose invalid structures unless the types prevent it

options.name: Headless behaviour plus styled layer
options.how: Publish hooks (useDialog, useCombobox) that provide behaviour and ARIA; styled components are thin wrappers.
pros: Teams with a genuinely different look reuse the hard parts
Accessibility logic exists once
cons: Two public layers to version
Headless usage can still ship off-brand UI

deepDives.choice: A layered approach with clear rules. (1) Styled components have a closed set of variants that map to design decisions, not CSS properties. (2) Complex widgets are compound. (3) Behaviour hooks are public for the 10% of cases that need custom visuals. (4) Escape hatches are limited: className for layout (margin, grid placement) and asChild for changing the rendered element, but no colour or spacing props. Every component also accepts native attributes and forwards refs. A new variant needs a design review. A team with a one-off need composes primitives instead of growing a prop.

deepDives.title: Distribution, versioning and codemods
deepDives.problem: 25 apps upgrade at different speeds, some run two versions on one page, and every breaking change costs ~50 engineer-days without help. Packaging choices also decide whether tree-shaking works and whether components from different releases fit together visually.

options.name: One versioned package with subpath exports
options.how: @acme/ui with one ESM module per component, sideEffects limited to CSS, semver for the whole library, released weekly with Changesets.
pros: One version number: components always match each other and the tokens
Tree-shakes when built with preserved modules and subpath exports
cons: A breaking change in one component forces a major for all
Teams can't upgrade one component alone

options.name: Per-component packages, independent versions
pros: Upgrade one component at a time
Small, focused changelogs
cons: Version-matrix hell: Dialog 5 uses Button 3 internals while the app uses Button 4
Duplicate copies in bundles; release tooling gets complex

options.name: Copy the source into each app
options.how: A CLI copies component source into the app; the app owns it from then on.
pros: Total freedom; no upgrade treadmill
cons: Fixes, including accessibility fixes, never reach the copies
Drift is guaranteed and invisible to the system team

deepDives.choice: One versioned package from the monorepo, with subpath exports and a bundle-size check in CI that fails if importing Button pulls in more than Button. Majors at most twice a year. The breaking-change protocol is deprecate, codemod, remove: a minor adds a dev warning and a lint rule; the codemod (jscodeshift or ts-morph) is tested on fixtures from real apps; the major removes the old API; a bot opens migration pull requests in every repo. The previous major gets security and accessibility fixes for 6 months. Class names are prefixed with the major version, so micro-frontends on two majors don't clash. If the org were one monorepo with one deploy, I'd skip semver and upgrade everyone in the same pull request.

deepDives.title: Accessibility guarantees
deepDives.problem: 'The library is accessible' means nothing unless it says what is guaranteed and what the app still owns. A perfectly accessible Dialog with no title, or an IconButton with no label, is still broken. And without automated checks, regressions slip in with routine refactors.

options.name: Manual review per release
options.how: An accessibility specialist reviews changed components with screen readers before each release.
pros: Catches what tools miss: reading order, announcements
cons: Slow and doesn't scale to weekly releases
Nothing stops regressions between reviews

options.name: Automated tests in CI
options.how: axe on every story in every theme; interaction tests (Playwright) for each keyboard model; contrast checks on token pairs.
pros: Runs on every pull request
Catches the most common machine-checkable issues: missing names, bad roles, low contrast
cons: Tools can't judge whether an announcement makes sense
False confidence if treated as complete

options.name: Accessible by construction
options.how: Types make labels required (IconButton needs aria-label, Dialog needs title); lint rules in apps flag misuse; components own focus management.
pros: Mistakes fail at compile time in the app
Pushes the guarantee to where the bug would be written
cons: Stricter types annoy teams at first
Needs escape routes for edge cases

deepDives.choice: All three, with a written contract per component: 'we guarantee roles, keyboard model, focus management, visible focus, contrast in all themes, reduced-motion support; you supply labels, headings and meaningful alt text'. Automated axe and keyboard tests gate every pull request. A manual screen-reader pass (VoiceOver with Safari, NVDA with Chrome or Firefox) is required before a component reaches stable status and for any change to its interaction code. Accessibility fixes are backported to the previous major, which makes them the strongest reason to upgrade.

deepDives.title: Measuring adoption
deepDives.problem: Leadership asks 'is the design system working?'. npm download counts say nothing: an app can install the library and still use it for one button. We need numbers that show real use, version health, and whether it makes teams faster and the product more consistent.

options.name: Static code scanning
options.how: Nightly AST scan of every repo: count DS component usages, deprecated props, and local look-alikes (raw button elements with custom classes, local Modal components, hard-coded hex colours).
pros: Objective and cheap (~50 min CI a night)
Finds exactly which files to migrate
cons: Heuristics for look-alikes miss some and over-count others
Says nothing about what users see

options.name: Runtime coverage sampling
options.how: Components add a data-ds attribute; a sampled script in production counts DS-rendered interactive elements versus all buttons, links and inputs on the page.
pros: Measures what users actually see, weighted by traffic
Catches legacy pages that scans undervalue
cons: Runs code in production; must be tiny and sampled
Needs privacy review

options.name: Surveys and delivery metrics
options.how: Quarterly developer survey (satisfaction, top pain points) plus time-to-first-screen for new features.
pros: Explains the why behind the numbers
Shows impact in terms leadership cares about
cons: Subjective, low response rates
Slow feedback

deepDives.choice: Static scanning as the backbone: coverage = DS elements ÷ (DS elements + look-alikes), version lag in majors, deprecated usages, per app and per team. Add runtime sampling (1% of page views) once the system is mature, because traffic-weighted coverage is the honest number. Run a short survey each quarter. Publish the dashboard openly, but use it to pick which teams to help, not to shame them. The first-year goals I'd propose: 70% coverage on top-traffic pages, no app more than one major behind, and accessibility violations in DS-built UI trending to zero.

failures: A token change breaks contrast in one theme
CI contrast check over all text/background token pairs per theme; visual diff required for token PRs; fast patch release and rollback via previous version.
Teams fork components because the API doesn't fit
Contribution model with office hours and a 2-week SLA on proposals; expose behaviour hooks; track forks in the scanner as look-alikes.
Tree-shaking silently breaks after a refactor
Size-limit check in CI per subpath import; fail if importing Button exceeds its budget.
Two majors on one micro-frontend page clash
Major-prefixed class names and a shared, backward-compatible token layer; tokens only ever add or deprecate, never rename in place.
Release introduces a regression in 25 apps at once
Canary releases tested in 3 pilot apps before latest tag; apps pin versions and upgrade through bot PRs that run their own tests.
The system team becomes a bottleneck
Federated contributions with clear review criteria, generated docs, and lint rules that answer common questions before they are asked.
scale: More frameworks (Angular, Vue, plain HTML): tokens and CSS are already framework-agnostic; add web components for the 10 most-used widgets, or thin framework wrappers over shared behaviour, instead of rewriting the library per framework.
More brands (white-label): brands become token files only; add a brand preview in docs and a contrast gate per brand; no component code changes.
Hundreds of contributors: component ownership per area, RFCs for new components, and automated checks so reviews focus on design intent, not mechanics.

followups.q: A team says the library slows them down. What do you do?
answer: Sit with them and find the specific gap: missing component, rigid API or slow review.
Fix the gap fast or give them a supported escape hatch (behaviour hook, composition).
Track it: if many teams hit the same gap, it's a roadmap item, not an exception.

followups.q: How do you decide what goes into the system?
answer: Rule of three: a pattern used by three or more teams, or needed for accessibility or brand consistency.
Start new components as alpha in one app, promote to stable after use in real products.
One-off patterns stay in the app, built from system primitives.

followups.q: How do you keep Figma and code in sync?
answer: Tokens have one source: Figma variables sync to JSON via a PR, or JSON pushes to Figma; pick one direction.
Component names and variants match between Figma and code, checked by a script reading both.
Docs show the Figma frame next to the live example.

followups.q: Would you build on an open-source headless library?
answer: Often yes: well-tested behaviour for menus, comboboxes and dialogs saves months.
Wrap it so its API isn't your public API, then you can swap it later.
Check bundle size, server-component support and accessibility track record first.

followups.q: How do you handle dark mode images and icons?
answer: Icons use currentColor so they follow text tokens.
Illustrations get theme variants or use semantic tokens inside SVG.
Photos stay as they are; avoid placing text directly on them without a token-based overlay.

mistakes: Starting with 60 components before tokens, so every component hard-codes values that must later be untangled.
Letting apps use primitive tokens or raw hex values, which makes theming impossible later.
Shipping breaking changes without codemods and wondering why nobody upgrades.
Claiming 'accessible' without saying what the app must still provide.

mid: Proposed design tokens as CSS variables with light and dark themes
Defined a Button and a Dialog API with variants and required labels
Listed accessibility basics: keyboard, focus, contrast, ARIA roles
senior: Designed primitive, semantic and component token tiers and banned primitives in apps
Explained the variant-vs-composition trade-off and set rules for escape hatches
Chose a packaging strategy and showed how tree-shaking is kept working (ESM, subpath exports, size checks)
Described deprecate, codemod, remove with real estimates of migration cost
Put axe, keyboard interaction and visual tests in CI
staff: Framed the problem as an adoption problem and quantified support load and migration cost
Designed adoption metrics (coverage vs look-alikes, version lag) and a dashboard used to direct help
Handled multiple frameworks and micro-frontends running two majors on one page
Wrote an accessibility contract that splits guarantees between the library and the app
Set a governance and contribution model so the team doesn't become a bottleneck
